imperious

im-PEER-ee-us -- from Latin imperiosus, from imperium ('command, authority'), from imperare ('to command'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Imperious is arrogant and domineering, acting as though one's authority should never be questioned.

The senior partner's imperious emails, always in capital letters and full of ultimatums, terrified every junior associate at the firm.

Example

The head chef ran the kitchen with an imperious hand, snapping orders and expecting every dish to appear exactly when she demanded it.

That commanding, top-down manner -- acting as if one's word is simply law, with no room for pushback -- is exactly what imperious describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overbearing: Overbearing describes someone who leans on the people around them — interrupting, insisting, smothering objections in ordinary conversation. Imperious has a grander, colder flavor: it is the manner of someone who assumes command, expecting obedience as a right rather than pushing for it.

high-handed: High-handed describes actions taken without asking anyone — canceling the picnic or rewriting the rules with no consultation. Imperious is about bearing rather than a single act: the lifted chin and commanding tone of a person certain no one may question them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

humble: having a modest view of one's own importance

deferential: showing respect for another person's wishes

Where it sits · how much control over others it demands — haughty → imperious → domineering

haughty vs. imperious: Haughty is milder than imperious on this scale: a haughty critic merely looks down on people and dismisses them, while an imperious boss goes further, issuing orders and expecting everyone to obey.

domineering vs. imperious: Domineering is stronger than imperious: an imperious manager expects obedience as her due, while a domineering one actively forces it, deciding what everyone does and crushing any pushback.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — imper-

root — imper-: to command (Latin (imperare))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of, having the quality of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin imperium meant 'command, supreme power,' and adding -ious ('full of') describes someone acting full of that commanding authority -- as though their orders should never be questioned.

Word Choice

Imperious describes someone's own commanding, top-down manner toward people below them -- contrast this with insolence, taught earlier in this unit, which usually describes disrespect flowing the other way, from someone lower in status toward an authority figure.
